item.title: HSC exam results to be published Saturday, how to check
item.description:
The results of this year’s Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations will be published tomorrow, Saturday.

Education Minister ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon will inaugurate the result publication activities during an event at the Secretariat at 11:00 am. Upon inauguration, the results will be simultaneously available at respective educational institutions and online.

According to previous announcements, the HSC and equivalent exam results were initially scheduled to be published on 29 October. The date was later revised to this Saturday.

The Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee announced that all concerned educational institutions must collect the board-published results via the websites https://eduboardresults.gov.bd and https://educationboardresults.gov.bd.

The board advised institutions to download and publish the results online by clicking the 'Result Corner' on those websites and entering the board and the institution's EIIN (Educational Institute Identification Number).

Examinees will be able to collect their results through the common website of the education boards and the individual websites of their respective boards. Students can also collect their results directly from their educational institutions.

Additionally, examinees can receive their results by sending a short message service (SMS) to 16140 from any mobile phone.

Example: Type HSC<>Dha<>123456 2026 and send it to 16140. Results will not be available at the Ministry of Education, education board offices, or newspaper offices.

Online applications for re-scrutiny and re-evaluation of answer scripts will be accepted from 1 November to 7 November. The application process and related guidelines will be published on the websites of the education boards.

This year’s HSC and equivalent examinations commenced on 2 July. A total of 1,270,583 regular and irregular candidates appeared for the HSC and equivalent exams this year, although a significant number of candidates were marked absent.

item.title: Bodies of 5 from Naogaon identified by DNA testing to arrive on Saturday
item.description:
The bodies of seven Bangladeshis, including five from Naogaon, who died in a fire at a sofa manufacturing factory in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, are scheduled to arrive in the country tomorrow, Saturday.

Their bodies are returning home nearly three months after the tragic incident.

The identities of the seven individuals were previously confirmed through DNA testing. Of them, five bodies will be taken to Naogaon and two to Natore.

The deceased from Naogaon are Shahin of Par Naogaon village in Sadar upazila, and Hasibul Hasan of Dubai village, Minhaz Pramanik of Madhyaboalia village, Masidul Sardar of Madhabpur village and Sagar Ali of Sahanagar village in Atrai upazila.

The two victims from Natore are Mohammad Shamim of Dighirpara village and Sharif Hossain of Khajura village in Lalpur upazila.

On 9 August, 16 Bangladeshi workers were killed in a devastating fire at a sofa factory in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The bodies of nine of the victims were repatriated on 27 August. The remaining seven were recently identified through DNA profiling, and their bodies are now being sent back.

Citing a notification issued by the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, Naogaon Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Saiful Islam stated that a ministry letter issued on Thursday confirmed the bodies are scheduled to arrive at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka at 8:05 am on Saturday via a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight.

A letter signed by Muhammad Rezaye Rabbi, Counsellor (Labour) at the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, stated that since all flights from Riyadh have been suspended since 10 October, the bodies were transported by road to King Abdulaziz International Airport in Jeddah.

From there, the bodies will be flown to Dhaka on a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight.

Copies of the letter have been sent to the concerned Deputy Commissioners, Upazila Nirbahi Officers (UNOs) and expatriate welfare offices to take the necessary arrangements.

Atrai Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Md. Moniruzzaman confirmed that the families of the deceased have been informed of the matter.

Meanwhile, the news of the bodies returning 2 months and 22 days after the accident has cast a fresh pall of gloom over the grieving families. While they wait to see their loved ones one last time, the agony of their loss remains profound.

The relatives are currently preparing to receive the bodies and bring them back to their respective hometowns for burial.

Parveen, wife of victim Shahin from the Par Naogaon Tazer Mor area in Naogaon town, said, "We have already lost him. The damage is done. Now, if the body is at least here in the country, the children will be able to see their father's grave."

item.title: PBI suspects Tahsif may have been strangled; probes local, foreign syndicate link
item.description:
The Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) suspects that former Air Force official Tahsif Souri may have been strangled to death, with investigators looking into the possible involvement of a powerful local and international syndicate.
PBI sources said Ahmed Shahriar Reza Deep, the friend who called Tahsif out of his home before he went missing, was taken into custody for questioning on Thursday night and brought to PBI Dhaka Metro North.
Investigators said they had obtained significant information from Deep, which is now being verified.
“Initially, we did not suspect robbery as his expensive watch and mobile phone were intact, and money was found in his pocket,” PBI sources said.
The sources added that although no visible injury marks were found on Tahsif's body, investigators suspect he may have been strangled. They are also looking into the possible involvement of multiple people and a powerful local and international syndicate.
He said the motive behind the killing was being investigated.
After Tahsif's body was recovered, Sub-Inspector Mostafizur Rahman of the Tongi River Police outpost prepared an inquest report.
According to the report, the body was recovered floating beside Rajabari Ghat on the Turag River at around 5:45pm on Wednesday.
In cases of unnatural death, police examine the external condition of a body and prepare an inquest report documenting their observations.
The report described Tahsif as approximately 5 ft 7 in tall, with black hair and a short black beard and moustache. His eyes and mouth were closed, and blood was coming from his nose. Both hands were bent in front of his head, with the fingers clenched into fists. His abdomen was swollen.
The report noted no visible injuries on his chest, abdomen, back, legs or genitals. He was wearing a black full-sleeved Kabli shirt and white trousers when his body was recovered.
The River Police's initial report also mentioned a wristwatch and an iPhone in his pocket. He was identified through the phone.
The body was subsequently sent to the morgue of Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital for an autopsy.
PBI headquarters Superintendent of Police Abu Yusuf said investigators were taking Deep to various places visited by the two men, including the motorcycle repair shop and the restaurant, to verify his account.
According to Deep's account, the two first went to a garage to have Tahsif's motorcycle repaired after leaving home. They then had dinner at Ququdodoo restaurant in Uttara.
After leaving the restaurant, they rode their respective motorcycles towards home. They remained together until the Uttara House Building area, where they parted ways at around midnight.
Deep claimed he returned home after that and knew nothing further about Tahsif's whereabouts.
Tahsif's father, Enayetul Karim, believes his son was killed as part of a planned attack.
He said Tahsif left home on Tuesday evening after receiving a phone call from Deep. At around 1:35am, Tahsif sent a message to his mother's mobile phone saying he was on his way home.
Speaking on Thursday afternoon, Enayetul said his son appeared to be in a hurry in the message. However, the family received no further information about his whereabouts.
A close relative, however, said the last voice message sent to his mother's phone did not sound like Tahsif.
Enayetul said his son was dismissed from the Air Force on disciplinary grounds. Tahsif later worked at the Bangladesh Cricket Board and Netra News.
He suspects his son was killed and his body dumped in the Turag River.
Tahsif had drawn attention over allegations that he filmed the viral video of then prime minister Sheikh Hasina leaving the country by aircraft from Kurmitola Airport on August 5, 2024.
During a podcast interview last July, Tahsif was asked whether he had lost his Air Force job for recording the video. He replied: “Might be.”
In the same podcast, he was asked about a report published by the daily Amar Desh claiming that an Air Force investigation into the video had uncovered the involvement of India's intelligence agency, RAW, within the force, and that Tahsif's name had surfaced in connection with the agency.
Tahsif dismissed the report, saying: “I think the report Amar Desh did is actually serving some propaganda.”
Following the publication of the report on August 4 last year, the Inter-Services Public Relations Directorate (ISPR) issued a rejoinder.
It said the report had claimed that two officers, including Tahsif, were forcibly retired over allegations of links with a foreign intelligence agency.
“In reality,” the ISPR said, the two officers had been retired through due process under the Air Force's prevailing laws and regulations in a different context, which had no connection with the allegations.

PM returns home after four-day Japan visit
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman returned home early on Friday wrapping up his four-day official visit to Japan aimed at strengthening bilateral ties, attracting investment and expanding trade and economic cooperation between the two countries.
“A Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight carrying the prime minister, his wife Dr Zubaida Rahman and members of his entourage landed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka at 2:48am,” said Prime Minister’s Deputy Press Secretary Shahadat Shadhin.
Earlier, the flight departed Narita International Airport in Tokyo at 10:55pm local time on October 29, he added.
At the invitation of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Tarique Rahman's visit featured high-level bilateral talks, the signing of cooperation agreements, discussions with Japanese business leaders on investment opportunities in Bangladesh, and visits to major industrial and energy facilities.
During the bilateral summit at the Japanese Prime Minister's Office on October 27, Tarique Rahman and Takaichi discussed strengthening the longstanding partnership between the two countries, with particular emphasis on trade, investment, energy security, infrastructure, technology, space research and regional and international affairs.
The two leaders also discussed a proposed private investment of one trillion Japanese yen (US$6.3 billion) in Bangladesh's energy, infrastructure and information and communication technology (ICT) sectors.
They discussed sending a Japanese team to Bangladesh to expedite progress on the investment plan.
Bangladesh secured pledges for two yen-loan projects worth a combined 46.56 billion yen, equivalent to approximately $295.5 million and signed six bilateral cooperation instruments during the visit.
The instruments included a grant agreement of up to 2.12 billion yen ($13.44 million) for a patrol vessel to strengthen Bangladesh's coastal security capabilities.
The two countries also signed memorandums of cooperation on improving the business environment, agriculture, the Employment for Skill Development Programme, and fisheries and livestock, alongside a letter of intent on climate change cooperation.
The two loan projects will support improvement of the investment environment in Bangladesh and the second phase of the Upazila Governance and Development Project.
Beyond the government-level agreements, 17 memorandums of understanding (MoUs) were signed between private-sector entities at the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO), according to State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir.
On October 28, the prime minister addressed the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Forum Dialogue at JETRO headquarters in Tokyo, inviting Japanese companies to invest in five priority areas: automotive manufacturing, energy, technology and space, high-speed rail and logistics, and agro-processing.
He pledged government support and reforms to improve the business environment.
During the visit, Tarique Rahman also met Japanese political leaders, development partners and business executives, including former prime minister Taro Aso, Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) President Dr Akihiko Tanaka, Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC) Governor Kazuhiko Amakawa and JETRO President Susumu Kataoka.
In meetings with representatives of major Japanese companies, including apparel giant Uniqlo, Mitsui & Co., Sumitomo Corporation and JERA, he explored opportunities to expand investment, establish factories, create jobs, facilitate technology transfer and develop skills.
The prime minister visited JERA's liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal and power plant in Futtsu and the Nittsu Logistics Hub in Ichikawa on October 27 to observe Japan's energy and logistics facilities.
On Thursday, he travelled to Nagoya and visited Toyota Motor Corporation's Motomachi factory and the Toyota Commemorative Museum of Industry and Technology, where he observed Japan's automotive manufacturing capabilities.
The visit comes as Bangladesh and Japan seek to expand economic engagement following the signing of their first-ever Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) in February 2026, providing a new framework for strengthening trade and commercial ties.
Japan has long been one of Bangladesh's major development partners, supporting key infrastructure projects, including Dhaka metro rail, the third terminal of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport and Matarbari deep-sea port.

item.title: Irene Khan: Women’s participation key to sustainable peace and security
item.description:
Bangladesh's Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Ambassador Irene Zubaida Khan, has called for meaningful women's participation in peace processes and decision-making, emphasising that grassroots initiatives are vital to preventing violence and building lasting peace.
Speaking at the UN Security Council's open debate on Women, Peace and Security (WPS) recently, she recalled Bangladesh's role as a key co-sponsor of Security Council Resolution 1325 and reaffirmed the country's commitment to the WPS agenda, according to the Bangladesh mission.
Irene Khan highlighted Bangladesh's National Action Plan on WPS, introduced six years ago.
After completing its first phase, Bangladesh is now implementing the second phase, with consultations involving stakeholders, particularly civil society and women's groups, remaining a key feature of the process.
The Bangladesh permanent representative underscored the importance of training and sensitising girls and young women on violence prevention and supporting their active participation in community-level mediation.
She stressed that grassroots efforts can prevent disputes from escalating into wider conflicts, noting that Bangladesh is prioritising these initiatives through government and NGO programmes.
Irene Khan also called for greater investment in women's organisations and human rights defenders, protection for women in conflict-affected settings, and predictable, sustained financing for peace operations and vulnerable communities.
Emphasising a gender-centred approach to security, she stressed that women must have a meaningful voice in peace negotiations, political leadership and decision-making.
The Bangladesh permanent representative urged the international community to translate WPS commitments into concrete action to advance inclusive sustainable peace.

item.title: Fishermen in Chandpur return to rivers as hilsa fishing ban ends
item.description:
Around 42,000 fishermen in Chandpur resumed ilish fishing in the Meghna and Padma rivers early Friday after a 22-day ban imposed by the government to protect mother ilish during the breeding season.
The ban on catching, selling and transporting ilish officially ended at 11:59pm on Thursday, allowing the fishermen to return to fishing after weeks of hardship.
District Fisheries Officer Fakhrul Islam said authorities maintained strict monitoring throughout the 22-day ban.
He said extensive drives were conducted across the rivers throughout the 22-day ban period to safeguard mother ilish.
Joint forces comprising the district and upazila administrations, the Fisheries Department, river police, the Bangladesh Coast Guard and the district task force patrolled the 70-kilometre sanctuary area day and night.
During this period, 238 operations and 72 mobile court drives were conducted in the sanctuaries.
These efforts resulted in the seizure of approximately 2.75 tonnes of mother ilish (egg-bearing ilish), as well as fishing nets worth Tk 2.71 crore, which were later destroyed.
A total of 161 cases were filed, and mobile courts collected approximately Tk 4 crore in fines for violations of the government ban.
Furthermore, 183 fishermen from Chandpur Sadar, Matlab Uttar and Haimchar were detained for catching mother ilish in the Padma-Meghna sanctuaries during this period. They were subsequently sentenced to imprisonment and/or fined.
To support those affected by the ban, the government distributed 25 kg of rice to each unemployed fisherman as temporary relief.
Many fishermen, however, voiced concerns that this assistance was insufficient.
Talking to UNB on Thursday, fishermen from Saformali, Lalpur, Anandabazar, Baharia, Dokanghar, Ramdasdi and Harina Ferry Ghat said rice alone was not enough to sustain their families.
They also demanded cash assistance alongside rice from the government.
Expressing their frustration, the fishermen said they were forced to take on debt just to manage their daily living expenses and were now deeply worried about how they will repay these loans.
"If at least Tk 3,000 per person were allocated, it would have provided some relief," they said.
The government imposed the 22-day fishing ban in the Padma-Meghna rivers in Chandpur from October 8 to protect mother ilish and boost future production of the country's national fish.

Section 144 imposed in Inani as gas fire burns for fourth day
item.description:
A fire fuelled by natural gas escaping from underground has continued for four days in Inani, Ukhiya, Cox's Bazar, prompting the local administration to impose Section 144 around the site to ensure public safety.
People have been barred from entering or staying within a 200-metre radius of the gas emission site.
The incident began on Tuesday, when a local resident, Abdullah, arranged for drilling work to install a tube well in his yard. Gas started escaping through the borehole, followed by flames.
As a precaution, families living near the site have been moved to safer locations. Authorities have also fenced off the area within a 200-metre radius with barbed wire and placed red flags to warn people.
Electricity supply in the area was initially suspended for safety reasons but was later restored through an alternative arrangement.
The incident has drawn crowds of curious onlookers, including tourists visiting Marine Drive and people travelling from distant areas.
SM Nafefun Arham, party chief of a geological survey team that visited the site, said the gas should be allowed to escape naturally for now.
He said the fire must not be extinguished and the gas flow must not be obstructed, as doing so could cause gas to accumulate underground and create high pressure. This could lead to an explosion, potentially putting a much wider area at risk.
He said the gas flow should initially be monitored for 15 days. If the flow gradually decreases, it may eventually stop on its own. If it does not, experts will be consulted on measures to control it.
Ukhiya Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Panna Akter said Section 144 had been imposed in the interest of public safety, prohibiting entry and movement within 200 metres of the fire's source.
She said people had also been instructed not to light fires, smoke or use matches or lighters in the area. The restrictions will remain in place until further notice.

item.title: Zverev 'on top of the world' after securing No. 1 ranking
item.description:
Alexander Zverev accelerated his ascent to number one in the world rankings for the first time in his career on Thursday as he beat Tallon Griekspoor 6-4, 7-5 to reach the quarter-finals of the Vienna Open.
The 29-year-old German was already assured of finishing the season top of the ATP rankings but, in the absence of current incumbent Jannik Sinner, two-time Grand Slam champion Zverev will now take that crown in next week's updated standings after winning his opening two matches in the Austrian capital.
"(It is) very special. To have the feeling to be on the top of the world is amazing," Zverev said.
"It is different than winning a tournament or a title, but it's such a special feeling to know that the No. 1 is going to be next to your name when the new rankings come out."
Long seen as tennis' nearly-man, Zverev has enjoyed a stellar 2026, breaking his major duck by picking up the titles at the French and US Opens.
Now he has broken further ground by becoming only the 30th man to claim top spot since the rankings were first published in 1973.
He will be aged 29 years and 196 days when Monday's new rankings are published, making him the second-oldest first-time number one after Australian John Newcombe.
Due to a knee injury the Italian Sinner decided to end his season at the start of October, opening the way for Zverev to dethrone him.
The big-serving Hamburg native ensured he did just that ahead of the season-ending ATP Finals next month by seeing off Martin Landaluce and Griekspoor in his opening two matches in Vienna.
Zverev needed to save four match points against Spain's Landaluce in his first-round match on Tuesday, but was much more comfortable as he defeated Griekspoor in straight sets to write his name into the history books.
He raced out of the blocks on Thursday, breaking the 30-year-old Dutchman in the very first game and then confidently serving his way into a one-set lead.
The second frame went to 5-5 before Zverev pounced on Griekspoor's serve to get his nose in front.
The match met an unexpected stoppage as Zverev brought up match point when a smash off the German's racquet caused part of the electronic board behind Griekspoor to malfunction.
But once the umpire covered up the problematic panel with a towel, Zverev then sealed his new ranking with an unreturnable serve.
Elsewhere, former world number one Carlos Alcaraz advanced to the last eight with a 6-1, 7-6 (13/11) victory over Georgia's Nikoloz Basilashvili.
The Spaniard will next meet American Tommy Paul for a spot in the semi-finals.
Another former top-ranked player in Russia's Daniil Medvedev also enjoyed success as he battled past Britain's Cameron Norrie in three sets.

item.title: Bangladesh reach Tier E final of FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival
item.description:
Bangladesh have booked their place in the Tier E final of the inaugural FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival after edging past Gabon 1-0 in the semifinals in Baku, Azerbaijan, on Thursday.
Naimur Rahman Ratul scored the decisive goal in the 14th minute to send Akbar Hossain Ridon's side into the final, where they will face the Central African Republic on Friday.
The young Bangladeshis have enjoyed an impressive run in the Tier E knockout competition after finishing fifth in Group G, bouncing back from a mixed group-stage campaign to move within one victory of a trophy.
Bangladesh began their campaign with a goalless draw against Wales before suffering a 3-1 defeat to Portugal. They subsequently drew 1-1 with Indonesia and lost 2-0 to Burundi before ending the group stage on a winning note with a 3-1 victory over Fiji.
The results placed Bangladesh in Tier E, where they began their knockout campaign with a dramatic victory over Seychelles. After a 1-1 draw in regulation time, Bangladesh won the penalty shootout 4-2 to advance to the round of 16.
They produced another penalty-shootout victory against Singapore, winning 4-3 after the match also ended 1-1.
Bangladesh then delivered their most emphatic performance of the knockout stage, thrashing Montenegro 4-0 in Thursday's quarterfinals. Mohammad Bayezid opened the scoring in the ninth minute, before Pavel Hasan struck twice in the second half, with Shibak Kumar Mali also finding the net.
Ratul's solitary strike against Gabon subsequently secured Bangladesh's passage to the final and kept their title hopes alive.
The final against the Central African Republic will take place at Baku Crystal Hall on Friday, with Bangladesh aiming to cap their historic campaign with silverware.
The tournament, being held for the first time, features 189 FIFA member associations and uses an eight-a-side format, with matches consisting of two 20-minute halves.
It is worth noting that Bangladesh are competing in the Tier E final, one of six performance-tier finals in the festival. The overall FIFA U-15 World Cup title will be decided in the Tier A final.

item.title: Inter and AC Milan unveil new stadium plans
item.description:
Inter and AC Milan unveiled their new "Generali Stadium" Thursday, which will replace the iconic San Siro stadium from the 2031/32 season.
It will be shaped "low in the body, and it rises up at either end" behind the goals, architect Norman Foster said during a press conference in Milan.
The design aims to bring spectators as close to the pitch as possible, with the stands behind the goals set at a steep 37-degree incline, said David Manica, a stadium specialist who collaborated with Foster on the project.
"The most important thing that we realised when we designed this project is that the San Siro is a feeling," he said.
"It's more than a building, it's a feeling, and everything that we needed to do here was to carry it into the (new) building".
Manica said the design team "started with proximity".
"We brought all the seats as close as possible to the field. They could not be any closer, it'll actually feel as though you're sitting on the grass," he said.
They also paid great attention to acoustics: the roof covers the stands, leaving only the pitch exposed, and is designed to "amplify the roar" of the fans, Manica said.
"This building is steeper than many other new buildings are built today, and that's intentional, because it allows us to bring those seats up and over the field as much as possible, and create that sense of intimacy and atmosphere," he said.
The stadium, sponsored by the Italian insurance giant Generali, will also be capable of hosting American football games, rugby matches and concerts.
"I want the crowd to come to the new stadium and to feel that excitement that they felt before, and to feel the building, living and breathing with them as it does currently," Manica said.
AC Milan and Inter paid 197 million euros ($219 million) to acquire the current stadium and its adjacent parking areas, where they intend to build their new, shared home.
The project for the new San Siro -- which will have a capacity of 71,500 seats, compared to the current 75,000 -- will cost the two clubs 1.2 billion euros.
Construction is set to begin in 2028.
Foster and Manica previously worked together on London's Wembley Stadium.
Milan's current stadium -- one of the most iconic in European football and often likened to a "concrete cathedral" -- is the largest in Italy.
But the venue, which opened in 1926, no longer meets the needs of spectators or the clubs, despite undergoing several renovations over the decades.
San Siro, also known as the Giuseppe Meazza Stadium, will be largely demolished once construction work on the new stadium nears completion.

Rafi sets four national records in two days at National Swimming
item.description:
Bangladesh Navy swimmer Samiul Islam Rafi made a sensational start to the 35th National Swimming, Diving and Water Polo Championship, setting four new national records in just two days at the Syed Nazrul Islam National Swimming Complex in Mirpur, Dhaka.
After breaking the men's 50m backstroke record on the opening day, Rafi continued his record-breaking run on the second day, setting three more national marks, including individual records in the men's 50m butterfly and 100m freestyle.
The Navy swimmer clocked 25.81 seconds in the men's 50m backstroke to better his previous national record of 26.05 seconds, set in 2025.
He then clocked 24.98 seconds in the men's 50m butterfly, improving his previous record of 25.15 seconds, before setting another national record in the men's 100m freestyle with a time of 51.80 seconds, bettering the previous mark of 52.42 seconds.
Rafi completed his four-record haul by helping Bangladesh Navy's mixed 4x100m medley relay team, alongside Mohammad Islam, Mukta Khatun and Fatiha Mahtab Maisha, clock 4:20.36 to improve the Navy's previous record of 4:24.55.
Rafi has also won four gold medals so far in the competition, capping an impressive individual performance.
His achievements followed an impressive outing at the 2026 Thailand Age Group Swimming Championships (25m) – Open/Senior Group G, where he won two gold and one bronze medal.
The second day of the national championship also witnessed several other record-breaking performances. A total of 14 new national records were established across swimming and diving events during the first two days, with six set on the opening day and eight on the second.
Organised by the Bangladesh Swimming Federation with sponsorship from Max Group, the October 28-31 championship features around 470 male and 102 female swimmers representing approximately 79 teams.

item.title: Can we do something about non-performing loans?
item.description:
For what appears to be decades now, non-performing loans (NPLs) have eaten away at the core of Bangladesh’s financial architecture.
What began as calculated political patronage, elite default culture, and systemic regulatory cowardice has essentially grown into a monumental crisis, with toxic debt dragging down the entire banking sector.
While the central bank’s newly unveiled 18-month strategy to accelerate bad debt recovery, tighten loan classification, and enforce strict restructuring is a welcome tactical pivot, blueprints on paper mean nothing if they end up gathering dust.
All eyes are now on Bangladesh Bank to prove that it finally possesses the institutional spine to deliver real results.
Previous administrations and toothless regulatory bodies have watched passively as willful defaulters looted public deposits, restructured bad loans endlessly, and hid behind political shields while commercial balance sheets bled out. State-owned and private banks alike became hollowed-out vaults of bad debt, eroding depositor confidence and starving productive sectors of vital liquidity.
Crafting another roadmap is easy; executing it against well-connected oligarchs and entrenched syndicates is the real test of state authority.
The central bank cannot afford any more false starts or half-measures. Implementing this 18-month plan requires aggressive, unyielding enforcement.
It’s time to hunt down willful defaulters without political bias, strip corrupt boards of control, and deploy fast-track judicial mechanisms to seize and liquidate defaulted assets. We are long past the times of regulatory leniency and debt forgiveness.
Restoring discipline to our financial sector is an existential necessity for our economic survival. The leadership at Bangladesh Bank must recognize that accountability cannot be postponed, and excuses will no longer be tolerated.
If this latest strategy fails to drastically reduce NPLs and restore transparent governance, the consequences for the broader economy will be catastrophic.

item.title: Beyond academic excellence: How Bangladesh can nurture students with an ethical compass
item.description:
Bangladesh is a land of enormous potential where its greatest asset is the intellectual energy, creativity, and ambition of its people, particularly its younger generation.
If we are to transform our country into a prosperous, innovative, and respected nation, we must invest in the quality of our human capital.
But a fundamental question deserves our attention: Are we preparing our young people only to succeed in life, or also to live a life of integrity?
Academic qualifications, professional skills, and technological competence are essential in today's competitive world. Yet these attributes alone cannot guarantee an honest business leader, an accountable public servant, a responsible citizen, or a compassionate human being.
Knowledge gives us the ability to act; an ethical compass helps us decide how and why we should act.
Bangladesh must therefore build an education system that nurtures both intellectual excellence and moral responsibility. Our objective should be to produce not merely successful graduates, but individuals capable of navigating life's moral dilemmas with wisdom, courage, and integrity.
Most of us grow up learning that honesty is a virtue, corruption is wrong, fairness matters, and others deserve respect. Yet real life often presents situations in which doing the right thing is neither easy nor convenient.
A student may witness a classmate cheating in an examination and struggle to decide whether to report it. A young professional may discover that securing a business advantage requires an unofficial payment. A public servant may face pressure to favour a relative over a deserving applicant.
These are not simply questions of knowing right from wrong. They involve competing loyalties, fear of consequences, personal interests, and social expectations.
This is where the distinction between moral instruction and ethical education becomes important. Moral instruction may tell students what is right. Ethical education must help them understand why it is right, recognize competing considerations, and develop the courage to act accordingly.
Young people cannot develop sound judgment merely by memorizing moral lessons. They need opportunities to question, reflect, discuss difficult situations, and learn from the consequences of their decisions.
Ethical development begins at home, long before formal education starts. Parents and family members shape attitudes towards honesty, responsibility, empathy, and respect. Children observe how adults behave, resolve disagreements, and practise the principles they teach.
The wider social environment is equally influential. When honesty is rewarded, institutions operate fairly, and wrongdoing carries consequences, young citizens receive a powerful message about integrity. Conversely, when dishonesty appears to bring success without accountability, the credibility of ethical instruction is weakened.
Schools and universities cannot work in isolation. They must be part of a broader national effort involving families, communities, businesses, civil society, and public institutions.
Educational institutions nevertheless have a unique responsibility. They bring together students from diverse backgrounds and provide opportunities to develop cooperation, fairness, critical thinking, and respect for others.
Character formation is not an optional activity to be undertaken after the syllabus has been completed. It is an integral part of education itself.
One important step is to strengthen the place of ethics in the national curriculum, from primary school through higher education.
This need not require a separate subject at every level. Ethical reasoning can be incorporated into literature, history, science, business studies, social sciences, and technology.
Science lessons can explore the responsibilities associated with scientific discoveries. Business education can examine conflicts of interest, fair competition, and corruption. History can encourage reflection on injustice and the abuse of power. Technology education can address privacy, misinformation, cyberbullying, and artificial intelligence.
Students should regularly encounter realistic dilemmas that require them to weigh competing choices. Is it acceptable to share an unverified story because it supports a cause they believe in? Should a company compromise environmental protection to reduce costs? How should a manager respond when a senior colleague requests an improper favour?
Complex situations do not always have simple answers. What matters is that students learn to identify relevant facts, consider who may be affected, evaluate competing principles, anticipate consequences, and justify their decisions.
Such an approach develops independent judgment rather than unquestioning conformity. It also teaches students that respectful disagreement, supported by reason, is essential to ethical thinking.
No education reform can succeed without teachers. They are not merely transmitters of knowledge; they are role models whose conduct can leave a lasting impression.
A teacher who treats students fairly, acknowledges mistakes, rejects favouritism, and listens to differing opinions demonstrates integrity far more effectively than a lecture on moral values.
Teacher training should therefore equip educators to facilitate ethical discussions, manage disagreements constructively, and encourage independent thought. Teachers must be able to address difficult questions without imposing personal prejudices or discouraging legitimate criticism.
Schools must also practise what they teach. If students hear that fairness matters but observe arbitrary punishment, preferential treatment or humiliation, the lesson becomes contradictory.
If they are encouraged to speak honestly but punished for respectfully questioning an unfair decision, they may learn silence rather than integrity.
Ethical education is credible only when institutional behaviour reflects institutional values.
In Bangladesh, considerable importance is attached to examination results, grades, certificates, and admission to prestigious institutions. These priorities are understandable in a competitive society where educational qualifications influence employment and social mobility.
However, when academic success becomes the overriding objective, the means of achieving it may receive insufficient attention. Excessive pressure can encourage cheating, unhealthy competition, fear of failure, and the belief that results matter more than learning.
We must reconsider how we define educational achievement.
Academic standards should remain high, but they must be accompanied by a culture that values honesty, collaboration, curiosity, responsibility, and perseverance.
Assessment can place greater emphasis on research, group projects, presentations, practical problem-solving, and reflection, supported by robust safeguards against plagiarism and cheating.
Students should understand that failure, when approached honestly, can be a valuable learning experience. A student who admits a mistake and tries to correct it may demonstrate greater character than one who achieves a higher mark through dishonest means.
The objective is not to weaken competition, but to ensure that competition does not come at the expense of character.
Ethical judgment becomes meaningful when translated into action. Educational institutions should provide opportunities for students to practise responsibility beyond academic exercises.
Community service, environmental projects, voluntary work, peer mentoring, and initiatives supporting disadvantaged groups can cultivate empathy and civic responsibility. Such experiences help students understand the circumstances of people whose lives differ from their own.
Schools and universities could organize student-led projects addressing waste management, public health awareness, digital literacy, educational inequality, and social inclusion.
These activities must not become another exercise for collecting certificates. Their value lies in meaningful participation, reflection, and accountability. Students should consider what they have learned, whose lives they have affected, and what they could have done differently.
Service, when approached thoughtfully, develops both social awareness and moral maturity.
In my earlier writing on public-private partnership in education, I argued that the government and the private sector can complement each other in expanding educational opportunities and improving quality. This principle is equally relevant to ethical education.
Businesses have a direct interest in developing employees and leaders who understand integrity, accountability, fair competition, and responsible decision-making. Universities, employers, professional associations, and civil society organizations could collaborate on practical ethics programs, internships, mentoring, and case studies based on real professional challenges.
Business leaders could share experiences involving difficult decisions affecting customers, employees, suppliers, and society. Professional institutions could help integrate ethical standards into medicine, engineering, law, accounting, management, and information technology.
Such partnerships, however, must serve the public interest rather than commercial priorities alone. Ethical education should not become corporate public relations or a vehicle for promoting particular interests.
The government must establish appropriate standards, while educational institutions retain academic independence and ensure equal access to opportunities. The private sector can contribute resources and experience, but nurturing responsible citizens remains a collective responsibility.
Rapid technological development presents new challenges. Today's students must learn not only how to use technology, but also how to use it responsibly.
Artificial intelligence can support learning, research, and creativity, but it raises questions about plagiarism, intellectual honesty, privacy, misinformation, bias, and accountability.
Students must understand the difference between using a tool to enhance their thinking and using it to misrepresent someone else's work as their own.
Digital citizenship should therefore be an essential part of education. Young people must learn to verify information before sharing it, respect privacy, recognize harmful online behaviour, and understand that digital actions can have real-world consequences.
Technology can provide answers with extraordinary speed. It cannot, by itself, determine which answers are fair, humane, or socially responsible. That responsibility remains with human beings.
Assessing the effectiveness of ethical education presents a challenge. Character cannot be reliably measured through a single examination or reduced to a numerical score.
Nevertheless, institutions can examine whether their environments encourage fairness, respect, inclusion, and constructive dialogue. They can assess how complaints are handled, whether students feel safe reporting misconduct, how academic integrity is maintained, and whether opportunities are distributed fairly.
Reflective journals, discussions, project evaluations, and peer feedback can help students examine their own decisions. These approaches should support learning, not label individuals as morally superior or inferior.
Bangladesh could develop a practical national framework for ethical education, supported by teacher development, institutional guidance, and periodic evaluation. The emphasis should be on continuous improvement rather than imposing a rigid or politically-influenced definition of morality.
Ethical education must encourage independent thought while respecting cultural diversity, constitutional principles, human dignity, and the equal rights of all citizens.
Ultimately, an education system should be judged not only by the number of graduates it produces, but also by the kind of society those graduates help create.
Bangladesh needs entrepreneurs who pursue profit without exploiting people, public servants who treat public resources as a trust, professionals who uphold standards under pressure, and citizens who defend fairness even when doing so offers no immediate personal advantage.
We need young people who question authority without disrespect, express disagreement without hatred, compete without dishonesty, and pursue ambition without losing compassion.
This is not an argument for replacing scientific knowledge, technological competence, or economic ambition with moral instruction. It is an argument for bringing them together.
The most valuable education combines knowledge with wisdom, ambition with responsibility, and individual achievement with a commitment to the common good.
The journey must begin at home, continue in our schools and universities, and be reinforced by the conduct of our leaders and institutions. It requires sustained commitment, not merely a policy announcement.
Bangladesh has every reason to aspire to world-class education. But world-class education must mean more than internationally competitive degrees, advanced laboratories, and employable graduates. It must also mean developing people who can be trusted with knowledge, authority, wealth, and responsibility.
Our ultimate objective should be to nurture a generation that possesses not merely the intelligence to succeed, but the ethical compass to decide what success should mean.
A nation advances most sustainably when its people know not only how to get ahead, but also how to do so without compromising their integrity. That is the education Bangladesh must strive to provide for its next generation.
A Gafur is a Private Sector Professional and Writer, and Former Executive Director, The American Chamber of Commerce in Bangladesh (AmCham Bangladesh).

item.title: 'Star Trek', 'X-Men' star Patrick Stewart dead at 86
item.description:
Patrick Stewart, the British Shakespearean actor who became a Hollywood megastar through roles in the "Star Trek" and "X-Men" franchises, has died at his home in Los Angeles. He was 86.
His death on Wednesday came after a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to an official statement on his social media accounts.
"His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre," the statement said.
The actor, who hailed from the northern English region of Yorkshire, trod the boards in Britain with the Royal Shakespeare Company and the National Theatre in London, and worked on British television.
But he rocketed into the pop culture history books in his mid-40s when he was cast as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," and then again as Professor Charles Xavier in multiple "X-Men" and related Marvel films.
A proud Yorkshireman, Stewart "wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love," Ian McKellan said of his "X-Men" co-star and dear friend.
McKellan, 87, recounted meeting Stewart in London and hearing about his "Star Trek" offer, warning him he may get lost in Hollywood and to think of his stage career.
"Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did."
Stewart was 47 when he debuted as Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," the first live-action television spinoff of the trailblazing late-1960s sci-fi series.
He effectively filled the boots of William Shatner's Captain Kirk -- to resounding success, both in the TV series and in several films.
Picard became known for a few catchphrases including "Make it so" and "Engage!"
But his move to America in 1987 was initially greeted with disdain by the Los Angeles Times, who wrote him off as an "unknown British Shakespearean actor."
Stewart later dubbed suggestions he was "slumming it" by moving into US television offensive.
He once called his Shakespearean bona fides "nothing but a preparation for sitting in the captain's chair of the Enterprise."
Stewart found further acclaim in the "X-Men" series, debuting in 2000 as Professor Charles Xavier, the founder and mentor of the mutant superhero team.
"For more than 25 years, he brought a gravitas and profundity to the role, earning fans across the globe," Marvel Studios said Thursday.
Longtime co-star Hugh Jackman, who played Wolverine, remembered Stewart as both "one of the greats of stage and screen" and "a tremendous friend and man."
Stewart is to make his final on-screen film appearance as Professor Xavier in "Avengers: Doomsday," set for release in December.
"What a heartbreaking week it has been," posted Shatner.
Stewart's death marked the second in days from the "Star Trek" universe, following that of Walter Koenig, who played Chekov in the original series.
Shatner said Stewart -- who most recently played Picard in 2023 -- brought "intelligence, grace and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did."
Stewart earned four Emmy nominations but never won. He did nab a spoken word Grammy, for his narration of "Prokofiev: Peter And The Wolf."
And even as he found success in Hollywood, Stewart's love of theater, and the bard in particular, never left him.
Between filming, he would return to the stage, winning two Olivier awards.
Shakespeare, Stewart said, "feels like a friend, someone who just went out of the room to get another bottle of wine."
The Royal Shakespeare Company called him "a colossus of both stage and screen and one of the finest classical Shakespearean actors of his generation."
Stewart was born on July 13, 1940 in the small West Yorkshire town of Mirfield, the third of three brothers in a working-class family.
His father, back from World War II and perhaps suffering from PTSD, would often beat Stewart's mother -- which prompted Stewart to later work with the charity Refuge, which specializes in domestic abuse.
The actor left school at 15, and studied at Bristol Old Vic Drama School beginning in 1957, making his professional acting debut two years later.
Prematurely balding, Stewart missed out on many of the young romantic leads but quickly slotted into theater life, joining the RSC in 1966 and staying there until 1982.
Any misgivings Stewart had about taking the Picard role in the "Star Trek" universe were mollified by the thought it would be a one-season failure.
He was wrong.
"It changed my life," he said.
Knighted in 2010, Stewart married three times: to Sheila Falconer, with whom he had two children; briefly to "Star Trek" producer Wendy Neuss; and most recently to American singer Sunny Ozell, 38 years his junior.

item.title: Advantage Australia as WTC series hangs in the balance
item.description:
Nathan Lyon ended South Africa captain Temba Bavuma’s resistance in the middle as Australia closed Day 3 of the third ICC World Test Championship Test in an advantageous position.
With a 40-run lead in the second innings, the Proteas are four wickets down in the second innings at the score of 140 and with Matthew Breetzke (19*) and Ryan Rickelton (8*) at the crease.
Australia centurion Josh Inglis believes his side is on top, with Nathan Lyon's late wicket of South Africa skipper Temba Bavuma a key moment in the game.
"I think we controlled the tempo really well in that last session," Inglis said.
"Although they were playing well, they weren't really getting away from us. I thought Gaz (Lyon) bowled brilliantly and looked threatening the whole time.
"When you work for a couple of hours and get the rewards right at the end, it's really satisfying,"
South Africa spinner Simon Harmer thinks there is still plenty of cricket left in the series decider and his spin may still have a big say across the final two days of play.
"If you look at how the wicket changed from this morning to this evening, it's been quite a dramatic change," Harmer noted.
"I think Mitchell Starc does a pretty good job of churning up the wicket (with footmarks).
"So yeah, I definitely think that spin is probably going to come into it a lot more than it has in the first two-and-a-half days."
The hosts had mounted an impressive display earlier on Day 3, restricting Australia to 429 after they began the day’s play with six wickets in hand and 330 runs on the board.
Inglis went on to complete an impressive century while Alex Carey also compiled 80 runs. For the home side, Marco Jansen and Harmer split seven wickets between them.
While Harmer finished with bowling figures of 4/104, Jansen continued his impressive run in the series with 3/60.
The performance comes on the back of the left-arm quick rising to the top of the ICC Men’s Test Bowling Rankings as well as the Test All-Rounders Rankings.
Trailing by 100 runs in the first innings, the Proteas were put on the back foot early on the innings as Mitchell Starc got rid of Aiden Markram in the third over.
A second wicket followed soon as Josh Hazlewood removed David Bedingham from the equation.
It was from here that South Africa’s highest run-getter in the first innings, Marques Ackerman and Bavuma, added crucial runs on the board.
The pair added 64 runs for the third wicket partnership as Ackerman scored his second half-century of the Test.
Starc however, got Australia right back into the game, snapping Ackerman. A final blow to the visitors was dealt by Lyon in the penultimate over as Bavuma returned to the dressing room.
Series schedule
First Test: 9-13 October, Durban (Australia won by 214 runs)
Second Test: 18-22 October, Gqeberha (South Africa won by an innings and 31 runs)
Third Test: 27-31 October, Cape Town
